newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Arab group calls for Security Council meeting.
newsitem.headline: Arab group calls for Security Council meeting.

text.p: The Arab group decided late Wednesday to call for a Security Council meeting to force Israel to rescind its decision to build homes for Jews in an area of East Jerusalem captured during the 1967 Middle East war.

The group's current chairman, Nasser al-Kidwa, the Palestine Liberation Organisation's U.N. observer, said an immediate meeting was being requested -- the U.N. term for the highest degree of urgency. The Arab Group is made up of the more than 20 Arab members of the United Nations.

But he said it might be delayed until later in the week or early next week since a new council president takes over on Saturday. Ambassador Njuguna Mahugu of Kenya, the president for February, will be succeeded by ambassador Zbigniew Wlosowicz of Poland.

The Arab group was reacting to the decision of an Israeli ministerial committee earlier in the day approving the construction of 6,500 homes for Jews on a tree-covered hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem called Jabal Abu Ghneim by Palestinians and Har Homa by Israel.
Some 2,500 homes are to be constructed in the first stage. Another 3,000 housing units are to be built for Arabs elsewhere in Jerusalem.
Al-Kidwa said a resolution would be submitted reaffirming the "illegality of the settlement activities and specifically requesting Israel to cease completely any settlement activities."
Regarding the new building project, he said: "We believe that the council should request Israel to rescind its decision and stop such construction in the area."

He said Israel acted "in defiance of the wish expressed by the council" Tuesday when, anticipating Israel's decision, it issued a statement expressing "concern at the new settlements policy of Israel in East Jerusalem and hoped that restraint and wisdom would prevail so as not to undo the peace process."
The council president had also called in Israel's U.N. charge d'affaires, David Peleg.

Al-Kidwa said it was "very unusual for any member state to take any decision in defiance of the Security Council next day after a message sent by the council through its president to that member state."
He hoped the council would meet "this week -- otherwise the first thing on the schedule of the new president."
"The request is to have an immediate meeting. Of course we also understand that there will be a change in the presidency and technical things of that sort."

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has sent urgent letters to U.S. President Bill Clinton, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, King Hussein of Jordan, and other leaders appealing for support in opposing the Israeli action.
The United States has said Israel's decision "further complicates an already complicated situation," while the European Union and Jordan have also protested.
Arafat is due in Washington Sunday on a previously arranged visit and will be in New York Tuesday.
Al-Kidwa said it was too early to predict whether Arafat might address the Security Council.
